speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) asked me the following question on the orders of the day on Thursday, March 7, as reported at page 1963 of Hansard:
Are newspaper stories correct that a certain number of Canada medals have been struck and have been issued to former cabinet ministers and others? If so, how many and to whom?
In 1944, as shown in the annual report of the Royal Canadian Mint, 14 specimen medals were struck and I may say at once I am informed that the word "specimen" was engraved on the rim of each of these 14 medals. These were delivered by the mint to the Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard), and the Secretary of State department can account for 12 of these 14 specimens. Two were transmitted to His Majesty and six were forwarded to the Department of National Defence in order that two might be placed in the permanent records of each of the three branches of our armed services. There are four which are still under lock and key in a steel cabinet in room 238 of the west block. There were seven with the word "merit" on the bar and seven with the word "merite" on the bar.
There were transmitted to the secretary of the Governor General, for transmission to the King, one with the English word on the bar and one with the French word on the bar. Three with the word in English on the bar and three with the word in French on the bar were transmitted to the Department of National Defence for the permanent records of the three branches of the service. There is 82715-130i
one with the word "merit" in English and three with the word "merite" in French still in safekeeping in the department of state.
It has not been possible to account for the other two. Searches have been made in the records at the archives and Laurier House and there is no reference whatsoever to these in the papers of the late Mr. King. I can assert quite positively that none of them has gone to any cabinet minister. They are still trying to ascertain whether there is any truth in the stories published by some newspapers that Mr. King kept one and sent one to Sir Winston Churchill. We have found no correspondence to bear out that story, but as a matter of fact there are two that are not accounted for.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of ihe Opposition):
maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF AUTHORITY OVER GAZA STRIP
speechtext:
I would like to ask a question of the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, in connection with a news report today by the United Press that Egypt has moved swiftly to re-establish its authority over the disputed Gaza strip.
Would the Prime Minister say what the latest information is regarding this matter, and also the degree to which the United Nations emergency force is to be permitted only through the whim or caprice of Mr. Nasser to be in charge in that area?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF AUTHORITY OVER GAZA STRIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have nothing at all to say about the whims or caprices of Mr. Nasser. I have made it clear several times in the house in answer to questions that the United Nations force has its responsibility to the United Nations, and that whatever arrangements between the United Nations and the government of Egypt were required

to be made or discussed were through the United Nations and not through the United Nations emergency force.
With respect to the report which the hon. Leader of the Opposition has mentioned, I have seen that news report, but we have no official confirmation of its accuracy, nor do I think it would be helpful to comment upon a newspaper report in any detail. It has been made clear that the actions taken on Egyptian territory or on territory which was, under the armistice agreement, subject to administration by Egypt would be decided after discussions with the government of Egypt.
I know that there are discussions which have taken place, and there are probably discussions which are going on, and I do not think it would be helpful to comment on newspaper reports about them.

maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF AUTHORITY OVER GAZA STRIP
speechtext: This is not comment on newspaper reports. But is it a fact that the situation is as described therein? Surely the Canadian Department of External Affairs, having regard to the fact that one-fifth of this force is Canadian, should have some information to place before parliament which is not dependent on newspaper reports but on communications from our officials abroad?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF AUTHORITY OVER GAZA STRIP
speechtext: Inquiries have been addressed to our ambassador in Egypt, and no answer has been received yet.

maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF AUTHORITY OVER GAZA STRIP
speechtext:
Then will the Prime
Minister say what attitude Canada intends to take regarding the stubborn stand taken by Egypt in insisting that canal tolls should be paid to Egypt rather than in pursuance of the plan reported by Britain, the United States, France and Norway whereby 50 per cent of the tolls would be paid into a trust fund. What attitude is the Canadian government taking with regard to this matter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF AUTHORITY OVER GAZA STRIP
speechtext:
It is true that by virtue of its advance of $1 million to the United Nations to cover part of the expenses of clearing the Suez canal Canada has acquired a special interest in the arrangements being made regarding the canal; nevertheless our interest can hardly be said to give us a position comparable with that of the major maritime powers whose stake in the future of the canal is of such dimensions that they are naturally taking the lead in trying to reach a settlement with Egypt through the good offices of the United Nations.
The government is in consultation with a number of the principally interested governments, but until their views have been received, and until there is some official indication of the Egyptian government's views on such issues as the payment of dues, the financing of the canal clearance and the

negotiation of a permanent regime, the government considers it would be definitely unwise to make a full statement. I can only say that the government has consistently supported the reasonableness of the proposition made by the principal users in respect of the way in which tolls might be handled until some more permanent arrangement has been found.

maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF AUTHORITY OVER GAZA STRIP
speechtext: Has that view been transmitted to the Egyptian government?

maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF AUTHORITY OVER GAZA STRIP
speechtext: That view has probably not been transmitted directly to the Egyptian government because we are not taking part in the negotiations that are now proceeding through the United Nations. That view has been transmitted to the Secretary General of the United Nations and it is through him that the arrangements are being discussed with the government of Egypt.

maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF AUTHORITY OVER GAZA STRIP
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a supplementary question to the Prime Minister arising out of those asked by the Leader of the Opposition. Does the Canadian government consider that Egypt is the owner of the Gaza strip?

maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF AUTHORITY OVER GAZA STRIP
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian government does not feel that it is its duty to announce considerations in the House of Commons upon all controversial questions that may arise anywhere in the world. The question of ownership or, I suppose, of the permanent sovereignty over the Gaza strip is a controverted question. The hon. gentleman's opinion or my opinion about what the correct legal solution might be is not going to have much bearing upon what it will be when it is finally determined.

maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF AUTHORITY OVER GAZA STRIP
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister happens to be the Prime Minister of Canada and, as such, he should be in a position to tell this house and the Canadian people what stand the Canadian government takes. Does it or does it not consider that Egypt owns the Gaza strip?

maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF AUTHORITY OVER GAZA STRIP
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have just said to the hon. gentleman that this is a controversial question upon which it is not our duty or our responsibility to announce what our position is nor would it be, in my opinion, of any help in its solution to have the government of Canada announce what its position is over any kind of lawsuit, especially an international lawsuit.

maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: EGYPT-REPORTED RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF AUTHORITY OVER GAZA STRIP
speechtext:
Has it any opinion of its own?
Inquiries of the Ministry

maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laureni (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: REPORTED ATTITUDE CONCERNING WITH- DRAWAL OF UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the stand has been
stated over and over again in answer to questions that have come to me from hon. gentlemen on the other side. I have stated that we recognize the sovereignty of Egypt

Inquiries of the Ministry over Egyptian territory, and that we recognize that the United Nations emergency force would not be stationed on Egyptian territory without the consent of the Egyptian government, just as no forces of other nations could be stationed on Canadian territory without the consent of the Canadian government; that consent had been sought and had been obtained, and had been sought and obtained for the purpose of doing a certain job. I have stated that it was our view that if the government of Egypt felt the United Nations emergency force should no longer be there Egypt should make its position known to the United Nations for the consideration by the advisory committee and then by the United Nations. So far as our troops are concerned, they will follow the instructions given to them by the commander who has been appointed by the United Nations. They receive no instructions or no directions directly from the Egyptian government.

maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: REPORTED ATTITUDE CONCERNING WITH- DRAWAL OF UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext:
Are we not consulted
at all? Is the Prime Minister not consulted in regard to the disposition that is to be made, particularly of the Canadian forces involved?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: REPORTED ATTITUDE CONCERNING WITH- DRAWAL OF UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext:
The Prime
Minister and the house were consulted as to the sending of Canadian forces who form part of the United Nations emergency force, and the Canadian government was advised that the acquiescence of the government of Egypt had been obtained. It was not sought and not obtained for the additions to the Canadian troops mentioned by the Minister of National Defence the other day. It is our view that consent having been obtained, we are justified in having our forces there, in virtue of our arrangement with the United Nations, and that it will be proper for them to remain there until they are informed by the commander appointed by the United Nations, under directions from the United Nations, that they are no longer required.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: FARM-STORED GRAIN
subsubtopic: REPORTED ATTITUDE CONCERNING WITH- DRAWAL OF UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext:
I shall have to take that question as notice. I have not attended the meetings of the United Nations general assembly nor have I been down there to hear everything that has been said in the

halls or corridors. I shall have to make inquiries about that. I do not know of any such statement having been made.

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration arising out of our lack of information. Can the minister inform the house what financial assistance is given to individuals who are giving housing or living accommodation to Hungarian refugees?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
maintopic: HUNGARIAN REFUGEES
speechtext:
I shall try, subject to the reservation that I may not be completely accurate in every detail, to give an answer, because I think there is a great deal of interest in the question. The department received a great number of offers of hospitality from Canadians, for which we were very grateful. Many of them were accepted. Many of these people desired no payment for this hospitality. In some cases it has been carried on much longer than might reasonably have been expected.
We have tried as far as possible to make it known that where people have stretched their own financial resources to a point which is not reasonable, the department is quite willing to provide the actual cost of subsistence in those cases until such time as the refugee or immigrant in question is able to support himself, and we hope that will be as soon as possible.
There are other cases where the department has made definite arrangements for boarding refugees, and that is done with other immigrants as well. I think it is well known to all hon. members that it is the policy of the department, during the first year that immigrants are in this country, if they become indigent or in need of help, not to treat them as persons who have become public charges and therefore are deportable, but instead to provide assistance to them until such time as they can support themselves again.

maintopic: HUNGARIAN REFUGEES
speechtext:
Well, sir, if the hon.
gentleman had read the return I made to a motion put by his leader a little while ago he would have seen that, in the case of those refugees who were admitted without being able to satisfy the immigration health requirements, the government did offer to provide whatever was necessary for them until such time as they were able to satisfy those requirements and become landed immigrants, in any province which did not make an agreement with us similar to the one which was made with Saskatchewan. maintopic: HUNGARIAN REFUGEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration which is supplementary to that which the hon. member for Moose Mountain asked, and to which a reply was given. maintopic: HUNGARIAN REFUGEES
speechtext:
We hope, sir, that at least 80 per cent of all the immigrants who come to Canada will never need any such assistance, and they are not encouraged to seek it; but it has been the policy for a considerable number of years to provide assistance to those who come here and who for some reason or other are not able to get established quickly or who lose their jobs at a certain season of the year until such time as they can get re-established during the first year.
As hon. members know, in most localities it is not possible without a year's residence to qualify for the ordinary local social assistance and that is the reason for this program. We try to make it reasonably well known so that immigrants will not hesitate to apply for help through fear that if they applied they might be treated as public charges, because it is our feeling that many very fine immigrants who will become good citizens do run into difficulties in the first year and it is to help over that year that this policy is carried out. The policy applies to all immigrants, though we do not feel the need should really arise very often in the case of sponsored immigrants because the sponsors do accept some responsibility.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the house has discussed this bill on several occasions and while the evidence of the committee has not been made available to members of the house, I am not disposed to allow this bill to stand as all necessary information is before hon. members.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Then I rise on a point of order. On Tuesday, February 19, as recorded on page 159 of Votes and Proceedings, which are the Journals of this house, the chairman of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines presented a report of that committee which included this paragraph:
Your committee recommends:
3. That it be empowered to print, for the use of the committee and of parliament, such papers and evidence as may be ordered by the committee and that standing order 66 be suspended in relation thereto.
That same issue of Votes and Proceedings contains this further entry:
By unanimous consent, on motion of Mr. McCulloch (Pictou), seconded by Mr. Cavers, the said report was concurred in.
The point I make at this juncture is that this house by a unanimous decision empowered the committee to print its evidence for the use of the committee and of parliament.
I would point out further that on Friday, March 8, when the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. McCulloch) presented the sixth report of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, that report read as follows:
Your committee has considered Bill No. 15 (Letter I of the Senate), intituled: "An act respecting Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company", and has agreed to report the said bill without amendment.
A copy of the evidence adduced in relation to the said bill is tabled herewith.
Then there appears on page 241 of Votes and Proceedings this notation:
The minutes of proceedings and evidence accompanying the said report recorded as appendix No. 5 to the Journals.
Mr. Speaker, as everyone knows, Votes and Proceedings is the name given to our minutes as they are recorded day by day, but at the end of the session, when they are put in a bound volume, they are referred to as the Journals. I draw to your attention

Private Bill
the fact that the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee in connection with this Bill No. 15 are referred to as an appendix to the Journals.
I hold in my hand, now, a copy of the most recent volume of Journals that has been printed. It happens to be the Journals for 1955, and I find there were 28 appendices to the Journals in that year. They are listed on pages 1053 and 1054 of the index to the Journals of 1955, and in every case the indication is that it was the printed evidence which was made an appendix to the Journals. I could take any one of these, but I will refer to a pipe-line one just to be in the same field. I quote:
No. 16. Trans-Prairie Pipelines of Canada, Limited. Bill No. 376, Printed evidence, re consideration of, in railways, canals and telegraph lines committee presented at page 651 as appendix No. 16.
I emphasize the point that it was the printed copy of the proceedings and evidence which was made an appendix to the Journals. I could read a dozen examples, but it is not necessary. I could refer to citation 168 of Beauchesne's third edition which makes it clear that the Journals are the official record of the house; also to citation 170 of Beauchesne's third edition which points out that the courts of the land have the right to have access to the Journals of the house, which are our official records.
The hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Fairey) wants up to proceed with this bill without our having before us something which is our right; because when they are printed and ready, the minutes of the proceedings and evidence before the committee on Bill No. 15 will be an appendix to the Journals, or to Votes and Proceedings, which are one and the same. The Journals are our official record, and I claim we should not be asked to proceed to consider this matter without having in our hands the actual document, appendix No. 5 which, as I have already suggested, will be the printed document when the records are complete.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that there is all the difference in the world between the evidence of one of our committees on a bill and the evidence in relation to divorce cases. The reason I mention that is because it used to be that we were not asked to proceed with divorce bills if the evidence was not iri our hands; but the time came when it was decided that that evidence, being evidence taken before a committee in another place, was not part of the proceedings of this house, and that therefore we had no right to claim it before proceeding to deal with a divorce bill.
We accepted that decision. Everyone knows, as far as that evidence is concerned,

that once we have finished with a divorce bill the evidence is sent back to the other place. This matter now before us is something different because it relates to the evidence of one of the committees of this house -a committee appointed by this house; a committee to which this house referred a bill; a committee which has printed its evidence on the basis of a motion passed in this house. And we are told by Votes and Proceedings that such evidence is an appendix to our Journals. We have not got it, and yet we are being asked to proceed.
On that ground, Mr. Speaker, I think that in all fairness we should not be asked to proceed with this bill today. As the hon. member for Victoria. B.C., knows, and I have checked this by consulting with some of my colleagues who were on the committee, there was a pretty contentious debate in the committee. At least one amendment was moved and defeated; there were votes and there was considerable discussion. I feel, therefore, that we have a right to read what took place before we enter upon a debate at this time. I had hoped that the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., would have responded to the request that he let the bill stand until another day-and there will be plenty of other days for him to proceed with his bill. But since he is not prepared to meet that reasonable request, I have no option but to place the matter before Your Honour as a point of order. It is my contention that until we have a printed record of what went on in that committee, which is referred to as appendix No. 5 of the Journals for this session, the official records of the house are not complete and therefore that we should not be asked to go ahead with this matter at this day's sitting.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Before the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Campbell) speaks, I would ask whether the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has any cases to refer to the Chair in which a similar point of order has been argued and decided by the Chair one way or another.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

This is a novel point. I do not even recollect any insistence being made upon the production of printed evidence before a second reading of a bill was proceeded with. In all my experience in the house since 1945 I cannot recollect any request being made in the house, except in the case of divorce bills, that the printed evidence should be made available to all hon. members before they proceeded to the second reading of a bill.

The hon. member has had a chance, so to speak, to prepare himself, and he has come to the house well prepared to put a certain point of order. If the house is to insist, as it usually does-and as the house, I think, may be entitled to-on an immediate decision on my part, I would say that I am almost prepared to give one, but I would like to have an opportunity of looking at this point further and, at least, for consultation with the Clerk.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word on this point of order. As hon. members of the house will recall, when this bill came up for second reading there was an amendment moved by the C.C.F. party that the bill should not be read a second time, but that the subject matter be referred to the committee. On that occasion I was one of those who

objected to that procedure on the ground that there would be no bill before the committee, but I said I would be prepared to support the bill going to the committee so that we might be able to hear the evidence from the witnesses, and so that members of parliament would then be able to know the facts. There is one thing I am going to ask hon. members. I have listened to them. Will they now be good enough to listen to me?
The point that has been raised is not an easy one and it is one about which, as usual,

I want to make a very sound ruling. I say that the printing of evidence is done by a committee, through an order of the house at their request, for the use of the committee. When I say that I am merely echoing citation 539 of Beauchesne, third edition, which is in these words:
In case a committee requires its evidence to be printed for its own use in the course of an inquiry, it will make a report requesting that this be done. Formerly it had to apply to the joint committee on printing, but this practice had to be abandoned in view of the fact that the printing committee consists of senators as well as members and the matter is one which concerns the commons only.
Therefore, in case a committee requires its evidence to be printed for its own use in the course of an inquiry it will make a report requesting that this be done. Immediately the hon. member will ask himself what I asked myself. Why is it that the report of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, to which the bill now up for consideration in committee of the whole was referred, is in the form found at page 159 of Votes and Proceedings? As found there, it reads:
3. That it be empowered to print, for the use of the committee and of parliament, such papers and evidence . . .
Whereas down below on the same page we find this. The standing committee on industrial relations asks that its evidence be printed but it asks for it in the following form which is the traditional form:
1. That it be empowered to print from day to day 750 copies in English and 250 copies in French of its minutes of proceedings and evidence, and that standing order 66 be suspended in relation thereto.
The wording in the report of the standing committee on industrial relations which appears in the Votes and Proceedings at page 159, the very same day, is in the traditional wording whereas the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines does not use the traditional wording. I can see a very good reason for that. So far as I can remember- and I think that at one time I was a member of that committee-that standing committee never asks that its evidence be printed except on extraordinary occasions. The standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines very seldom request the services of shorthand reporters. So far as I can recall, I have never seen a bill going through that committee where the proceedings were being taken in shorthand. We hear the officials at various sittings of the committee and they answer questions, and the evidence is not printed. I am informed by the Clerk that it may be that the clerk of that committee prepared the report which was submitted to the house and approved, as it appeared at page 159 of the Votes and Proceedings, in that
Private Bill
form. But as I say, that is not the traditional form. The traditional form is the one exemplified in the report which appears at the bottom of the page; and the report which appears at the bottom of the page is quite in line with citation 539 of Beauchesne's third edition which contains the words, "a committee requires its evidence to be printed for its own use".
There is another point I should like to bring to the attention of hon. members. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) himself stated that the committee had asked for the printing of 650 in English and 150 copies in French. If the hon. gentleman could state that as of right he must have the evidence before he can proceed with the second reading of a bill, he should at least make sure that there are enough copies in both languages to proceed with the bill; that is 265 copies in English and 265 copies in French. That is so with respect to any measure that comes before the house. The rule is to the effect that all documents that we deal with here must be translated into the two languages.
I should also like to point this out to hon. members. If we were to agree with the reasoning that was presented to us by those who have placed the point of order before the chair, then towards the end of the session when several committees have had matters referred to them, if we had to wait for the evidence to be printed before we could deal with the legislation that has been reported from these committees, and evidence printed in both languages, we would have to wait sometimes one week, two weeks or three weeks, and sometimes more than that; and in cases of French evidence we would have to wait for from one to two to three months, so I am informed by the officials at the table. What that would mean is this. Any bill reported from the various standing committees towards the end of the session could not be proceeded with until about three months, four months or five months in order to get the evidence.
The point raised by the hon. member is, as I said,-and I think he will realize it himself-a novel one. In my experience I never heard it raised before. It is a matter of courtesy, I would say. The hon. member has asked the sponsor to allow the bill to stand because he would like to see the evidence. Presumably he is not a member of that committee. The sponsor of the bill says no. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) raises the matter as a point of order. After consultation with the Clerk at the table I must come to the conclusion that under our practice or under our rules it has never been contemplated that we should have to wait for the evidence to

be printed before we take up second reading, study in committee of the whole or third reading of a bill. I am satisfied that citation 539 of Beauchesne's third edition states the position clearly, namely that the minutes of evidence of a standing committee are printed for their own use and once they are reported, they become a permanent record of the house of the proceedings of that committee. But if we were to state that they are required for the study of any of the stages of a bill, I would say that we would in fact be placing in our book a new rule to the effect that the bill had better not be reported before the evidence is ready and we would have the result I outlined a few moments ago, namely that in certain cases the committee could not report the bill because the evidence could not be printed for three or four months.

Mr. Chairman, like those hon. members who have spoken earlier this afternoon I regret that hon. members of the house have not had an opportunity to review the evidence presented to the committee. If they had they would have discovered that the evidence adduced in the committee was not such as to justify the demands of this company and its sponsor in this chamber that its shares be split five to one. At the extremely interesting sessions which we had the alleged reasons kept changing and I think I should refresh the memories of hon. members with regard to the position of the shares of this company at the present time.
A total of five million shares were authorized by the act which passed the house in 1951. Of those five million shares, some
1,500,000	have been issued and of those 1,500,000, less than 500,000 have been offered to the general public. These shares are of no par value. We are now asked to authorize the splitting of the shares in order to make the total authorized shares 25,000,000.
The first reason given in the committee was that the company wished to have a wide distribution of its shares. I recall that at that point I asked one of the officers of the company why they wished to have a wide distribution and the answer I got was that it was good public relations. I must confess that that surprised me considerably because the president of the company had told us already that this company has no dealings whatever with the general public. In fact he stressed again and again that it is merely a transportation company which transports oil belonging to certain oil companies to the customers of those companies. When I pressed the president to be a little more explicit on the subject of public relations he suggested that the place at which they came in contact with the public was when they were trying to get rights of way for their pipe line. I pointed out that their present pipe line is already on a right of way, but he pointed out in turn that they still have another pipe line or perhaps more that they intend to build and for which rights of way will have to be negotiated with the public.
He was unable to tell me just why the owners of the land through which the line would go would be particularly favourably impressed if the company officials were able to tell them that they had five times as many shareholders as they have at the present time. I made what I thought was a reasonable suggestion to him, that the owners of that land would be interested solely in the

prices they were going to be offered for their land in order to permit the pipe line to go through it.
We were told that this particular measure has been brought forward on the advice of the financial advisers of the company. I asked what was the advice of those advisers. I would presume that the financial advisers of any company would give advice calculated to improve the financial position of the company and I wanted to know just how the financial position of this company was going to be improved by splitting the shares five to one. I was unable to get any satisfactory answer.
Then there was an even more fundamental question to be asked and to which we got no answer, and that was whether or not there will be any actual effect of a wider distribution of the stock if this house in its wisdom sees fit to authorize the split five to one. The officers of the company were unable to tell us that they had received any information from their shareholders that any of them would be prepared to place any of their stock on the market after the split took place. The officials of the company also told us that the company has no intention of placing on the market any of the existing 3,500,000 shares which now lie in the company treasury.
Those rather ambiguous and evasive statements on the part of the company officials led me to pursue this matter of public relations again and I followed up a lead offered by the hon. member for Bow River who with a deplorably cynical attitude suggested that perhaps the public relations referred to had something to do with the impact upon the public mind of the net return per share of this company. He had suggested, as I say in a deplorably cynical manner, that perhaps this was what the company had in mind, that things would not look quite so bad if the net return per share was only one-fifth of what it had been in the last year. Being of rather duller mind than the hon. member for Bow River, although perhaps equally cynical, I seized on this. I thought that perhaps the hon. member had something.
Therefore I looked into the figures showing the net return and found that in 1955 they had a return, after all taxes and depreciation had been allowed, and they were very generous with those two items, of something over $3 million or approximately $2 per share on the 1,500,000 shares which were in the hands of the public. In the following year 1956 things picked up tremendously because the company had a net return of over $7 million on the 1,500,000 shares in the hands of the public.

Then we asked the treasurer of the company if he would care to make an estimate of the possible net return in the current year of 1957. That gentleman did so, perhaps rather inadvisedly from the point of view of the case he and his colleagues were presenting to the committee, and he told us that judging by the returns for the first two months of this year he would estimate that the net return this year would be at least $10 million, being 50 per cent over last year which was 100 per cent over the year before.
I think this brings us to the milk of the coconut, or perhaps I should say the juice in the melon because the statement was made, and reiterated several times by the president, that this company has not yet been declared a common carrier. He was asked on a number of occasions whether the rates of his company were subject to any regulation and he said no, that they had not been declared a common carrier. The thought occurred to me that possibly if they feared the creating of bad public relations that certainly would raise a feeling among the unfortunate oil consumers of British Columbia when they received another increase in their bills-they have had two in the last two months-if that increase was coupled with a net return per share for 1956 of some $4.75 and a possible net return of about $6.60 in 1957. There might then well be a public demand that this concern be declared a common carrier having its rates subject to regulation by a federal authority.
However, the four witnesses before the committee were unable to see anything whatever in the suggestions of this sort that were made to them, and they fell back, time and time again, on the statement that it was just a general matter of public relations they were concerned About-that it did not really matter whether the stock was divided into five or ten parts, or how it was divided; they wanted to see that it was more widely distributed in the interest of good public relations. We were told that this decision was made on a recommendation from the board of directors to a shareholders meeting. It was described, Mr. Chairman, as a well attended shareholders meeting, but I do not think that phrase was repeated after we elicited the information that out of some
4,000	shareholders there were 50 present, nor was it repeated after we elicited the information that something like three-quarters of the shares of this company are held by corporations and one-quarter by private individuals.
There is every reason to believe, Mr. Chairman, that the corporations which hold the majority of the stock in this company
Private Bill
are, in the main, oil companies who are interested, naturally enough, in the transportation of their product to the market, and I cannot imagine that they would be really very concerned about a wide distribution of the stock; I cannot imagine that that would cause them very many sleepless nights. I can only reach the conclusion, Mr. Chairman, that it was concern for the very large net returns per share which are now made evident wherever the company makes a public statement. It was, of course, pointed out to us that even after the shares have been split into five, and we have, instead of 1,500,000, some 7,500,000 shares out, a perusal of the company's balance sheet would reflect the profit situation of the company accurately to anyone who wished to study it. That is quite true, but the fact remains that the general public have the habit of looking at the net return per share and this is much more convenient, for instance, to the Langley Greenhouses with whom some of us have been having correspondence, and who have had their fuel bills raised twice in quick succession-it is much more convenient for them to read that the company gets, instead of $6.60 a share merely one-fifth of that per share; and very few people look behind that into the actual financial setup of the company.
For that reason, Mr. Chairman, I think the house should be very chary of permitting this sort of stock market manoeuvre to take place. There are, I think, only two explanations for this demand on the part of the company. One is the concern I have suggested, namely that it will place their net profit situation in a more respectable and acceptable light with the general public. As to the other reason, hon. members may recall the suggestion I made during the second reading of this bill that there might be some capital gain to be acquired by those who now hold larger units. If they are split, and if shares of much smaller value become the subject of active stock market trading, the prices of the split shares might rise, bringing considerable financial benefit to those who own them. Under our present economic system and under the present government such forms of income are virtually untaxable and must be very attractive to those who otherwise may have to pay out big sums in income tax.
For these reasons I think there is no justification whatever for this house agreeing to the demands of this company. The fact that it is a common and disreputable practice of a great many corporations in this country with whom this house does not have to deal, because they do not operate under act

of parliament, does not alter the situation here, when we have a case which is actually our responsibility.
Because this company was established by act of parliament we are responsible for the activities of this company in the future, and I suggest to you, sir, that to agree to this is to agree to what will be, in effect, a gross misrepresentation of the tribute which this company is drawing from the oil consumers of British Columbia.
I am not going to touch on another aspect of this company's operations, because I imagine it will be dealt with by other speakers; I refer to the relative importance of the Canadian and the American markets for the production of this company. However, I would urge all hon. members of the house, in spite of the fact that they have been deprived of the privilege of reading the proceedings before the railways, canals and telegraphs committee, to regard this measure with a very great deal of suspicion and doubt, and decide that a company which has done very well for itself in the past and which, apparently, has determined to do even better for itself in the future by means of price increases which I doubt can be justified even on the basis of the Suez canal closure, should not be permitted to mislead the public -they should be made to reveal their real position. And if there is a public outcry demanding that this company should be designated a common carrier, then that is all to the good, because I think such a project should be a common carrier and should be subject to the control and regulation of this parliament.

Of course, the officials of the company went to great lengths to explain that they had to have good public relations. I admit immediately that good public relations are a good thing in any company. Public relations are very good for the chartered banks, too. You will remember that the last time the Bank of Toronto brought out a report it showed an over-all profit of 24 per cent on their paid-up capital. It is not good public relations to have that widely known, so after issuing further shares and taking out their reserves they got it down to about 4 per cent per share, and that was as a result of watering stock. That is good public relations for them but the public just do not know how they are being gypped. That is the only word I can think of and I will have to put it on the record.
I suggest, too, that so far as the public relations of this company are concerned, the thought that is running through the minds of the officials of this company is not that they want to create good public opinion but to deceive the public by splitting the shares five for one. Assuming they pay a dividend of $1, as they did last year, and assuming there is no greater profit and no additional money for distribution the amount of the dividend, provided the shares are split five for one, would be brought down to 20 cents.
I say to you that the public are more apt to accept as reasonable the 20-cent share than they would be to accept the dollar share. What will happen in a few years if these dividends are $5 a share or $6 a share? The public is going to say to themselves-and rightly so-that the transportation charges that these pipe line companies are charging for the transportation of oil and gas products are out of all reason and that there should be some reduction in the price of these fuels to the public. Instead of that, we find the price of gas and oil products going up all the time. That fact is due in part at least to such manipulation of shares as we find we are being asked to agree to in this bill. From our point of view as members of parliament I think that is poor public relations and should not be permitted.
I do not want it to be said, Mr. Chairman, that I am against private enterprise. This party, the Social Credit party, are staunch private enterprisers. But let it always be said that we are against exploitation of the public. For that reason and for the other reasons that I have indicated we just cannot support this bill splitting these shares five to one. Some people seem to take this thing a little bit lightly. They may not view it as seriously as we do. I am inclined to think that when the amendment was submitted in committee to divide the shares not one to five

but one to ten, that was done from a standpoint of humour rather than good sound thinking. When you split the shares one to ten, you do not necessarily create any wider distribution than would be created by splitting them one to five, or very little. But you would cut the dividend down per share a great deal more than would be done on the basis of a split of one to five. That is why I think the amendment was not put forward with too much serious consideration. Of course in the committee I was obliged to vote against the amendment. I should have liked to join in the fun but from the standpoint of principle I could not see how we could support a split of one to ten when we were objecting to a split of one to five; and we were objecting to it on the grounds I have indicated this afternoon to the house.
I am sorry that more members of this house are not here to hear the arguments that are put forward by members who were on the committee. When the vote is called, of course, the members will come in to vote. Maybe some of them, had they been here to hear the story completely from all sides, would be in a much better position to make a decision on the basis of sound judgment rather than just as a result of persuasion from some of their friends. I would hope that the members of this house would not pass this bill. I would hope that the company would reconsider their stand and possibly, if the necessity arose, when they had issued a substantial portion of these 3,500,000 shares that they now hold in the treasury-which number will be increased to 16 million when the split takes place-or when they had issued some of those on the market, would come back to this house and ask for further consideration for an increased issue of stock because they need the money. Then I would be one of the first to agree that they should have it if they need it. I think they would be well advised, if for no other reason than that of good public relations, that they do that very thing and not try to force this bill through for a one to five split.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
If we go back for a moment to read again the explanatory note that accompanied this bill when it was first introduced to this house and then compare that with the story of some of the evidence given to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, I think we cannot help but come to the conclusion that not only is the proposal contained in this bill, as was suggested by the hon. member for Bow River, an attempt to deceive the public but that it was also an attempt to deceive the members of this house. The explanatory note says this: The reason for the proposed subdivision is that the company wishes to achieve a wide distribution of its stock among investors in Canada.

As I recall some of the evidence that was given to the committee by the president of that company, when this question was raised he said, in so many words, that the company really had no particular interest in whether this stock split was made or not, that it was not really anything that was going to affect the company as such. Then when the question was asked as to whether this thing had been requested by the shareholders of the company, we were informed that no such request had been made by the shareholders to the board of directors. When we asked whether the board of directors had decided it themselves, we received only very vague explanations as to how, when and why the board of directors had apparently decided to submit that proposal to a meeting of the shareholders of whom we were informed there were 5,806, of whom something over 50 attended what was described as a largely attended meeting of the shareholders of the company.
I recall that, at an earlier stage in the discussion of this bill, some of the facts and figures which were placed on the record by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam were called into question. I am hoping that the figures I intend to use in the course of my remarks will not be called into similar question. As has already been pointed out, we are under the disability of not having in our hands the official evidence and an opportunity to study it. Under these circumstances it is perhaps fortunate that some of us who were in attendance at the committee meetings tried to take a few notes. As far as I know, the figures I am going to use are those that were actually given to the committee, although I do not feel that I can use them with the same degree of confidence I could if I had had the actual printed evidence before me. The figures and facts, as those of us who sat in the committee recall, clearly indicate that the original purpose which was set forth as being the purpose of this bill, and which some of us at an earlier stage were inclined to doubt, certainly is not the real purpose that is behind the introduction of this bill.
You know, sometimes the housewives of Canada are criticized for being overly anxious to keep up with the Joneses. Apparently that same philosophy extends into the august financial realms of the country in which the people who own and operate pipe lines live. Actually, as I recall it, the principal reason given to us for the decision to introduce this bill in parliament for splitting the shares was that it is the thing other companies do and therefore this company did not dare do anything different from any other company. They thought it was the correct thing
Private Bill
to do, so they wanted to occupy the time of parliament by introducing a bill to split their shares five for one. Apparently, it is something like the latest fashion in Easter hats. When one achieves a certain standing in the financial and industrial world, one has to follow the fashion in Easter hats.
Actually, so far as I am concerned I think that some of the facts that were given to us in the committee did help to reveal that, not only in the operations of this particular company but also the operations of other companies which they claim they are following, we have the root cause of some of the serious disabilities under which the average citizen of this country is labouring today. This is not, therefore, the kind of proposition which this parliament should support. The figures, as they were given to us, show that the current book value of the assets of this company amount to $104 million, and that a large part of the original financing of the company was gained not through the issue of shares but through the issue of bonds bearing fixed interest rates. This has resulted in the actual book value of the shareholders' equity today being approximately $14 per share for the 1,504,928 shares that have been issued from the treasury of the company.
The figure given in the committee as to the quoted value of the stock on the market that day was $117. Well, Mr. Chairman, you can readily see that the shares which had a real value of $14 were being sold on the market for $117, which is fantastically above their real value in terms of the assets of the company. If these 1,504,928 shares were to be sold at $117 on the market, they would sell for $176,076,576 according to my calculation, whereas if the shares were sold at their real value of $14 per share they would be worth $21,066,992. The difference, therefore, between the real value of those shares and the currently quoted market value is $155,009,784. This represents, in the hands of these shareholders, over $155 millon worth of unearned purchasing power.
In other words, if the shareholders sold all the shares at that price they would have over $155 million going out into the market places of the country buying goods and services, with what to me is an obvious result- obviously, an inflationary pressure upon the economy. Some may say, well, all the shareholders are not going to go out and sell their shares at that amount; that is merely a paper value which does not represent actual purchasing power. Probably that is quite true, but it does represent potential purchasing power of an inflationary nature within the economy.

Private Bill
We were told in the committee that in recent months the actual number of shares in this company being traded monthly totalled something like 2,500 shares. The fact that these 2,500 shares are traded at a market price of $117 means that the people who are selling these shares at $117 are selling them at $103 over their real value according to the book value of the assets of the company. Each time one of those shares is traded in the market somebody is getting $103 in unearned purchasing power which can be used to buy goods and services or which can be reinvested. This means that these 2,500 shares which are being traded on the average each month put into the economy $457,500 every month of inflationary purchasing power. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that is one of the reasons why this house should not deal with the introduction of this kind of bill lightly.
I think all of us realize full well it is highly unlikely these shares are going to be traded at one-fifth of their present market price when they go back on the market. In the normal course of events these shares are going to creep up within the foreseeable future to something like the same market value as that at which they are selling today. We all know that has happened in the past. We cannot say with any certainty it is going to happen in this particular instance, but if these shares are split and if they do come back on the market on the basis of their present market value, that would mean that instead of 2,500 shares-assuming the same volume of trading-putting only $457,500 per month of what I described as inflationary purchasing power into the economy, there would be $2,287,500 per month going into the purchasing stream. And that, Mr. Chairman, multiplied by the activities of other companies which are doing the same thing, gives us some idea of the magnitude of the social and economic problem that lies behind this business practice.
As far as I am concerned this is a valid reason why hon. members of this parliament should not acquiesce in this kind of business transaction. Some of us cannot help but contrast this sort of activity and its resultant increasing of purchasing power in the hands of the few people who own these shares with the problem that most Canadians are facing today in keeping their incomes in line with what they must pay for the goods they need to maintain an ordinary home containing some of the goods that our modern industrial system is able to turn out so freely.
When we think of the people who are struggling along to buy for themselves some furniture, or a new washing machine, or whatever it may be and are compelled to

go out and deal with some of the financial institutions we have discussed on other occasions; the struggle they have to get enough purchasing power in their hands to buy the goods that are being produced, and compare this with what is being put into the hands of the people who carry on this sort of manipulation, then I suggest we have a situation which gives us good reason to pause and reflect.
This type of transaction and all that accompanies it, with all the dangers to the normal functioning of our economy that are inherent in it, cause me at least to remember what happened back in 1929. I am fully aware that people like myself are called prophets of gloom when we suggest anything of this nature could possibly happen again. But, Mr. Chairman, let us remember what took place and realize that it can occur again if this sort of practice becomes even more fashionable, to the point where inflationary pressure on the economy is such that when a crisis occurs the tremendous paper value of these shares suddenly plunges down to less than the real worth of the share certificates. If this happens on a large scale we know it will create a very drastic and sudden fall in the available purchasing power in the country. The result of course would be closed factories and people out of work. The $900 million in our unemployment insurance fund is not going to seem very large if that should happen.
These are some of the things we must think about when we are asked to pass what the sponsor referred to as a simple bill at the time he introduced it for second reading. I would suggest that if in the majority we were not so ready as we apparently are to go along with this sort of thing the Minister of Finance would not be asked questions, as he has been in the last few weeks, concerning the problems people are experiencing in financing their homes. The $457,500 per month these people have to spend is perhaps one of the reasons there are no investment funds available to build houses at reasonable rates of mortgage interest. All these things are tied in together and are matters about which we should be thinking.
As far as I am concerned the evidence that was given to us in the committee has only served to strengthen the conclusions I reached on the basis of the knowledge I had of the matter prior to sitting as a member of that committee; therefore, Mr. Chairman, I urge the members of this house not to acquiesce in the continuance of this so-called fashionable trend among companies in this country which, because they have a monopoly at least within their own area of operation, are

able to draw tremendous sums from the people who have to rely on the facilities they provide.
I suggest we should reject this kind of proposal, that we should tell them to get on with the business of transporting oil, and as long as they attend to that business and run it efficiently we are not going to begrudge them some reasonable measure of return on their enterprise as such. But if they are going to come here and suggest that their concern is to create a situation which in the over-all can adversely affect the financial stability of this country, we should tell them to forget about it.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I sat as a member of this committee for the better part of a day trying to make up my mind whether the passing of this bill was in the interests of Canada, and after having listened attentively to the evidence adduced I came to what I felt to be a reasonable and fair decision on it. I concluded that I must oppose the bill.
In the first place, the officials of the company who appeared before the committee gave one reason and one reason only for coming to this House of Commons to have this bill passed. If the reason they gave is the only reason they have for coming before this house, then I must conclude that it is just humbug. I say that after thinking the matter over very seriously. There must be some reason that we were not able to drag out into the light for their coming to parliament at this time, but the only reason given by the officials of the company was that they wanted better public relations.
It is stated in the explanatory note that a relatively high market price discourages investment by the small investor, but I do [DOT]not think they were interested in new investors. Therefore there must be some other reason for them coming before this house.
The only reason they gave was that they wanted to create better public relations. I cannot understand why a company of this size, which is making such good money and which is dealing with only a small group of people, those who are shipping oil in a large way from Alberta to the coast and on down south, would have to have good public relations scattered far and wide. If like the mail order companies they were dealing with people all over Canada then I would admit there was some reason, but they are dealing with only a comparatively small number of people, and for the life of me I cannot see why they should take the trouble to come before this house and take up the time of the house as well as of the committee in presenting their case.
Private Bill
There is no question but that this company is making big money, and I submit it should be declared a common carrier. At the present time there are no restrictions upon the rates it can charge. It can charge as much as the traffic will bear. If it were declared a common carrier the rates could be set by the board of transport commissioners for the protection of the consuming public.
I live close to the province of Alberta, and know that the carriage of oil and gas in large quantities through these pipe lines has made a considerable difference in the price of those products. I submit that this company and any other company that is transporting oil and gas by pipe line should be declared common carriers in order that some supervision may be exercised over the rates they charge. I am opposed to the bill and am going to vote against it. I hope the committee will turn down the bill.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I also am one of the unfortunate members who was not on this committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and therefore have not available the information which was supplied to the members of that committee. As a result I am somewhat handicapped, though I have had the good fortune to have at my disposal during the past hour or so a transcript of what was said in the committee.
At the beginning of my remarks I want to compliment two hon. members of this house who are not members of my political party upon the attitude they took. One is the hon. member for Bow River; the other is the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond asked a large number of pertinent questions, but he did not get answers to very many. They always managed somehow or other to sidetrack them.
In the light of some of the mail I have been getting, this is far from being the simple bill the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., described it as when he first called for second reading. The operation of this pipe line is supposed to be beneficial to the people of Canada, especially the people of western Canada. I have here some figures which indicate what has happened since this pipe line was built. This information was sent to me by a large consumer of oil, Langley Greenhouses Limited. They show that on February 14, 1956, barely a year ago, the price they paid for bunker 46, which I assume is the grade they use, was raised from 8.9 cents to 9.3 cents per gallon. There were other raises in price on March 6, 1956, and November 24, 1956; then finally on January 22, 1957 the price was increased from 10.8 cents to 11.2 cents per gallon. This

Private Bill
was an increase of 2.3 cents, or 25 per cent over the price charged previous to February 14, 1956.
When the working people of this country ask for a wage increase of 20 per cent many people seem ready to hit the roof, yet these companies levy an increase of 25 per cent within 12 months without any hesitation. These people also supplied me with the information that one of the larger shareholders of the company, either directly or indirectly

that is, Imperial Oil Limited-had indicated that its 1956 earnings were 11.3 per cent over its 1955 earnings. I should like to see the day when the old age pensioners, the workers and the farmers could indicate a net growth in their income of 11.3 per cent or 25 per cent.
The construction of this pipe line was supposed to help the consumers of oil, and a lot of people threw out their old heating systems and put in oil heating systems. I have here proof of what I myself have had to pay in British Columbia. On December 7 last I paid 17.9 cents per gallon, and on February 26 of this year that price had gone up to 18.6 cents per gallon. Since I am a member of the House of Commons perhaps I should not worry too much, but here is what Mrs. Anna Larsen, who is 76 years of age and who lives in Burnaby, has to say:
I see the oil company make so much money I would think they could sell us the oil cheaper. Instead of that Feb. 1 they advanced the price from 21.9 to 22.6. I did not know before that the oil from Alberta went through the Suez; it must. It is too hard for us old people to split wood, looks like we will have to.
Before hon. members get too worried over the confidence of the investors of Canada in this company I should like to refer to a letter received from a small investor who lives in Strong Pine, Saskatchewan. He tells me that for some time he has been trying to invest a little bit of money in this type of enterprise but has never been able to get anywhere in obtaining shares at anything near the $10 level at which they were first issued. I suppose the reason is that he is a small investor and is not in on the ground floor with his broker to such an extent as to be regarded as a valuable customer.
The people have been disappointed, and that is to be expected from a sifting of this evidence. As I said before, I have not had time to sift it thoroughly, but it does seem obvious that the owners of the oil, the owners of the pipe line, the owners of the refinery and the owners of the bulk of our filling stations are one and the same group of people. 1 want to sound a word of warning. I do not think any party in this house would like to see the day arrive in Canada

when this vast and mushrooming oil industry became more powerful than the government of Canada itself.
I think it has been mentioned that in British Columbia we have a private company, the British Columbia Electric Company, which makes and unmakes governments at will. Let us beware that such an octopus does not arise on the Canadian national scene which can make and unmake political parties at election time and ensure the election of whatever government it pleases. I am not saying this has happened, but I believe the danger is there. We are expressing our regrets at what we see with respect to the power of the oil monopolies in the life and development of the peoples of the Middle East, and we hope the same thing may not happen to us here.
My main complaint about the proposal is not so much about the money that the company is making but that this oil pipe line has done so little for the development of our Canadian economy. We looked forward to a great expansion in employment on the west coast; we looked forward to the cost of oil being reduced because a cheaper method of transportation had been found. Our contention at that time that the public interest would best be served under public ownership was not acceptable, and it was again turned down by this house this year. However, even under private enterprise some of these purposes could have been served had there been any wish to serve the cause of national development.
One could hardly expect the final owners of this pipe line to be keenly interested in national development when those final owners, despite the evidence to the contrary which was submitted, are not Canadian owners. There was listed before the committee a large number of shares which afe held in Canada as compared with the relatively fewer shares held in the United States. What the witness did not bring out was the fact that these Canadian oil companies owning most of the shares in Canada are only subsidiaries of the larger American oil companies, and therefore the predominating interest of the major oil companies would always take precedence over the interest of the people of Canada as a whole.
The reason advanced for asking permission to split shares is subject to some other grave doubts. When we look at the debate that took place in 1951 it is evident that we have very good cause to question any of the utterances the company makes, and any of the reasons it puts forward to the committee. Almost every pledge that was given in 1951 has been violated, and almost every prediction that was made about the potential

results that would accrue to Canada and Canadians has not come true.
At that time, I notice, an announcement was made to the House of Commons that the B-A Oil Company was about to build a $10 million refinery on the shores of Burrard inlet. That prediction was not fulfilled, and I am very much afraid that if this government remains in office much longer the $18 million refinery now being spoken of will also not be built within Canada. The statistics the witness placed on record before the committee proved that at the present time there is more oil being exported to refineries in the United States than is being refined in Canada, and that is certainly a direct violation of any understanding given to the House of Commons and also to the committee of this house back in 1951.
I notice that in the March 1 issue of the Financial Times-maybe I should not refer to it, because as far as the economic scene in Canada is concerned it is the least reliable newspaper we have-there is an article which contains a long list of projected expansions in refining capacity in the United States; in the state of Washington, in Oregon and in the state of California. I do not see any mention in the article of any proposed expansion in the refining industry in Canada. The companies who own these pipe lines should be made by the parliament of Canada to understand that they have a responsibility to the country which owns these reserves, and especially to the people in the country that owns these reserves.
I notice the company is engaged-and I see this also in the minutes-in an expansion program. An expansion program for what? They say they are able to provide all the needs of the Canadian refineries, and if they are able to supply all those needs that indicates it is the same old story again, that the article in the Financial Times is perfectly accurate; that a huge expansion is planned south of the border, and that the capacity of the pipe line must be increased in order to meet the needs of the expanding oil industry.
I am not opposed to a prosperous United States of America. However, the responsibility of this parliament is, in the first place, to a prosperous Canadian nation. The small investors of Canada have not been given a break in this enterprise. The company is engaged in the export of an irreplaceable natural resource. The company is not helping to provide employment opportunities for Canadians. The company has violated practically every agreement and understanding it has ever made with the Canadian parliament or a committee of the Canadian parliament, and I am indeed surprised that a member such as the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.)
Private Bill
who is, I know, held in such high esteem by the average constituent in the city of Victoria, should even lend his name to this racketeering which is as old as the stock market itself, and have the nerve to try to pilot a bill of this sort through the Canadian House of Commons.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think it is significant that although this bill has now been under discussion for some little time, not one hon. member on the government side has been able to say a good word for it so far. Even the sponsor will, I am sure, find it very difficult to go back to the voters in British Columbia and explain-

speechtext: That will be my trouble, not yours.

speechtext: You just want to filibuster the bill.
