speechtext:
-and explain to them that it would be good for the people.
In 1951 the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines had the original bill before it, and at that time, as found at page 86 of the report of the proceedings of the committee, the following was pointed out:
Our proposal is to build the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line, which Mr. Laing has so thoroughly described lor .you previously. It is a line running Irom Edmonton to Vancouver via the Yellowhead pass. It is an all-Canadian line, of 24 inches in diameter, and approximately 715 miles in length. The line will have an ultimate capacity of the order ol 200,000 barrels a day, and the immediate capacity will be approximately 75,000 barrels a day. If the proposal meets with your agreement and the different regulations are completed at a sufficiently early date, it is proposed to commence the line in July of this year and to complete it by the 31st of December, 1952.
I find, Mr. Chairman, that you were a very alert member of the committee at that particular time. You asked this very appropriate question:
Might I ask, Mr. Chairman, why there is such a difference between the estimated initial capacity and the ultimate expected capacity? Is that due to marketing, or what?
The witness replied:
Actually it is due to the initial demand and the engineering arrangements that are made for that line. When it first goes into operation it will have pumping stations designed to handle the immediate requirements, having regard to the estimated production from Alberta. The ultimate capacity would be obtained by the addition of further pumping stations on the line as the market requirements and production go up.
Then my colleague the hon. member for Kootenay West also had a very pointed question. He asked:
When we were discussing the Trans-Canada Pipe Line Company, the company in question agreed to an amendment of section 6, that it be provided for and stipulated that the main pipe line of the

Private Bill
company would be entirely within Canada. Might 1 ask the witness if he would be willing, when we come to section 6 of this bill, to have a similar amendment inserted at the appropriate place in this bill?
The witness replied:
We would welcome such an amendment, Mr. Chairman.
Then I find that the Deputy Speaker, who was also a member of the committee, asked some very important questions. In the report of the proceedings of the committee I find the following at page 89:
By Mr. Robinson:
Q. Perhaps I can lay the groundwork for it. Mr. Blair, are you familiar with the wording of the amendment which Mr. Herridge mentioned?
A. Yes, I am familiar with the wording as it was stated in the other hearing.
Q. And it is that wording you say you will welcome with open arms?
A. We welcome it for the reason that it in no way conflicts with our intentions. Our intention is to build the line from Edmonton to Vancouver with the terminal there. The pipe line will be entirely in Canada and we will finish it in that manner.
Q. I would just like to get your idea of the effect of the amendment should your intention change in the future. Should your intentions in the future come to be along the line that you would like to extend your pipe line into the States, do you think, or would you consider that you would be bound by that amendment and that you could not do so?
A. I would understand that amendment, sir, as meaning that we were confining our operations to Canada, in accordance with our present plans. We do not visualize any pipe line outside of our own country.
Q. Let me put it this way. Suppose you want to go into the United States, do you think that you would have to come back to parliament and ask to have other powers? I just want to get your idea on how far the amendment would bind you?
A. I do not know that I am in a position to answer that legal question. We are just not planning that sort of development.
Q. Perhaps another witness would answer it for me.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
I still think that the discussion is a little premature and, if you do not mind, we will postpone it until we come to the legal aspects, and until we actually have the suggested amendment.
Apparently without any further reference to parliament it has been possible to extend the line into the United States. In the Financial Times of March 11 I note that there are to be large refinery extensions in the west coast area and, unfortunately, across the line in the state of Washington. The report reads in part as follows:
Richfield Oil Corp. has just taken up a 1,000-acre site at Everett for another major installation. The availability of Canadian oil from nearby Vancouver via tanker and through branch pipe lines is one of the major reasons given for the west coast refinery concentration in the Puget sound area but industry sources state that by no means all the new requirements following upon the completion of the new refineries will be met by imports of Canadian oil.

Texas Co., for instance, has imported oil holdings, through subsidiaries in Sumatra, and is currently bringing about 11,000 barrels daily to its California refineries.
It would appear, Mr. Chairman, that in spite of the assurance given to the appropriate committee at that time the major development is now to take place in the United States. The witnesses who were before us the other day reported that as of January of this year-I am sorry I do not have the official transcript available, but I made these notes at the time-there were 71,150 barrels of oil transported daily through the line for Canadian use, compared with 84,859 barrels for United States use and 33,000 plus for tankers. Apparently a good deal of the tanker oil would make its way to California for the development of industry in the United States.
In February Canadian consumption was 76,000 barrels daily, United States consumption was 74,500, and tanker export was 26,500.	In	March there are to be	78,500barrels daily for Canadian use, 67,000 for the United States and 33,000 for tanker export. However, it would appear that commencing	in	April we are to use	less	of theoil per	day	in Canada than will	be used inthe United States. The estimates are 72,500 barrels in Canada and 76,000 in the United States.	In	May the estimates	are	74,000
barrels for Canadian use and 76,000 for the United States, and the same for June.
I think it was the hon. member for York West, Mr. Chairman, who indicated that if there was any suggestion that the passing of the legislation would build one more mile of pipe line or bring in one more gallon of oil everyone would be in favour of it. But it is significant that the sponsor of the bill and the officials of the company could not say a good word for the proposition except from the point of view of public relations, and when they were cross-examined they indicated that as far as the public are concerned it makes very little difference to John Doe whether there are 500, 5,000 or 5 million people who are interested in this particular proposition. What John Doe is concerned about is whether he is paying too much for petroleum products, and whether this is going to increase or decrease the price of petroleum products. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that every member who votes for the passage of the bill is voting for an additional toll to be placed on the consumers of petroleum products in Canada.
At this point I should like to pay a compliment to the hon. member for Bow River. When this matter was before the house previously he deferred passing judgment. In spite of the representations made by a number of hon. members he said he had

an open mind. He said he would like to have the bill go before the standing committee, and that he would make up his mind after hearing the witnesses. After hearing the witnesses and cross-examining them, the member for Bow River thought there was no good reason why this particular proposition should be accepted by parliament.
Over the week end I did a little research. I was reminded of the problems we had on our doorstep at the time of the investigation into price spreads during the early 1930's. The practice of stock-splitting is not new. We were forced to concede to the officials of this company that if they were operating entirely within a province they would be permitted to engage in this anti-social activity without any restrictions.
But since it is a company that is operating across provincial and international boundaries it must come to parliament for a charter, and must come to parliament to get permission for this stock split.
I was reminded of very disturbing information that was made public back in the thirties. At page 2800 of the proceedings and evidence of a special committee I find a very interesting discussion by one of our former colleagues, Mr. Ilsley. The latter played a very important role in Canada in maintaining price controls and in preventing profiteering and racketeering during the war period. At that time, as reported at page 2800 of this evidence, Mr. Ilsley was crossexamining some of the officers of the Robert Simpson Company. This company had quite a long examination. One of their officers was asked by Mr. Ilsley as follows:
By Mr. Ilsley:
Q. Mr. Adamson, assume the case of a man who got one share in 1902 for which he paid $100. A. Yes.
Q. Assume that the gentleman followed that share through to 1925 when he got his cash, then he had 5 shares? A. Yes.
Q. By 1925? A. Yes.
Q. And for which he got $150 apiece, which made $750? A. Yes.
Q. And he also got 5 other shares which he exchanged for 15 shares? A. Yes.
Q. And those 15 shares he sold in 1929 for $150 apiece which is $2,250; the $2,250 plus the $750 makes $3,000, which he got in 1929 for an original investment of $100 with his cash dividends every year in the meantime? A. Yes.
Q. That is the whole story is it not? A. Yes.
But that was not quite the whole story. Mr. Sommerville, counsel for the committee, wanted to get a little bit more information that he thought should be put on the record. He asked:
Q. Now then, what were the dividends received? A. The dividends received were: . . .
And then a list is given of the percentages. These dividends worked out on quite a generous basis. Starting in 1903 they were
Private Bill
at a rate of 6 per cent. Then they went up to 8 per cent in 1914. In 1917, when young Canadians were fighting for freedom the percentage rate of these dividends went up to 10 per cent. It was 10 per cent in 1918, and went up to 11 per cent in 1919 and to lli per cent in 1920. Then Mr. Sommerville asked this question:
Q. Yes? These were on each share. If the holdings at 1917 were 5 for 1 and the dividend declared was 10 per cent it is equivalent to 50 per cent on the original investment? A. Yes. In addition to that there were the bonds and preferred shares.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that having had a public inquiry back in 1934 in order to try to focus public attention on the very antisocial effect of share-splitting, share-watering and speculation of this sort, the parliament of Canada should be the last organization to put its seal of approval on this particular proposition.
Along with the hon. member who is sponsoring this bill I will admit that there are pipe-line companies which have an even worse record than this one. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, I believe it was two weeks ago today, referred to the Westcoast Transmission Company, where 500,000 shares offered at 5 cents each were picked up, the present value of which is $35 a share; so that for every dollar put into the Westcoast Transmission Company back five years ago there has been a capital gain of $700.
However, I submit that this Trans Mountain company has no mean record as to multiplying the returns to those who get in on the ground floor. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni used the figures that were given to us by the officers last Thursday, I think it was. The officers of the company mentioned the fact that the very interesting discussion we have had in this house with regard to Trans Mountain has probably been a factor in these shares going up in price. In Saturday night's Daily Star I noticed that the high has now been reached of $119. These shares have had a low of $104 in 1957, with a high of $119. If the shares were to be sold now at the prices being offered, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni would have to revise the figures upwards. It would appear to me that the 1,504,928 shares which are outstanding at the present rate of $119 would bring in $179,086,432.
The officers of the company told us that the book value at the present time is about $14 a share. So if you took away the book value of $21,068,992 you would have a capital gain of $158,017,440. I appreciate the fact that if we were to multiply these shares five times, so that instead of having 5 million shares we had 25 million, we muddy the water and make it possible for organizations

Private Bill
of this sort to do the sort of thing the Robert Simpson Company did during the period 1902-1929, the period which was under review by a parliamentary committee in 1934.
I think it is still as plain as A, B, C that since we are not making any plans to build any more pipe line as a result of this legislation, and are not making any plans to encourage development or to build refineries, the only justification for taking up the time of parliament is to permit a few speculators to profit, though probably not to go as far as the people in Westcoast Transmission who were, I admit, in much better shape. For every dollar you put into Westcoast Transmission on the basis of 5 cents a share, you now have $700. But here for every dollar you put into Trans Mountain you have only about $12-the cost was $10 and the price is $119-or $11.9.
The officers of this company were able to present quite an interesting story about the success of their operations. They pointed out that in the last year-that is in 1955-their net profit, after paying all taxes, was just over $3 million. In 1956 their net profit they estimate to be a little bit less than $7 million. I was able to do a little calculation over the lunch period at that time, and on the basis of $7 million net which they had last year- and that was earned by operating their line at about 70 per cent capacity, and even without making any allowance for the fact that if you were to operate it at 100 per cent capacity you would not necessarily increase your returns to your directors and your personnel-it would appear that they are almost certain to have a net after all taxes of between $10 million and $11 million this year. It would appear that if they were prepared to declare half this net as a dividend to their shareholders they would be able to pay a return of around 50 per cent per annum to those who put in their $10 per share just a very short time ago.
Now I realize that if instead of paying $5 per share, the company issues five shares for every one that is outstanding and only pays $1.25 per share or $2 per share, they will take the attention of Canadians away from the fact that oil prices in the Vancouver area are going up, allegedly because of the trouble in Suez. Then the Canadian people might not say the reason we are paying more for our petroleum products in the British Columbia area is that Trans Mountain Pipe Line, which should be a public carrier, wants to further split its shares and make it possible for some of its investors to make an almost unlimited profit.

I submit, Mr. Chairman, that with a very inflationary situation on our doorstep we cannot afford to set an example here by suggesting it is quite legitimate for people to come to parliament and take the time of the other place and this chamber to get legislation through which they do not attempt to say is going to increase our production, or is going to improve our dollar position, but is merely going to make it possible for those interested in playing the market to make fabulous profits.
I note that this measure received very short treatment in the other place. It was presented on Thursday, January 24, when it was moved by Senator McKeen. After a very brief statement the motion was agreed to, the bill was read a second time and referred to their standing committee on transport and communications. I have made inquiries about getting printed copies of the proceedings of the Senate committee on transport and communications, but I am informed that it is not the practice to publish those minutes.
I would have thought that since their minutes have not been published, and in view of the fact that the hon. member who sponsored this bill intimated that it had received careful consideration in the committee of the other place, when the measure came back to the Senate some of the hon. senators who thought this was a proposition for the public good of Canada would have made some comments about it. However, the Acting Speaker read the report of the committee, and after the report was adopted the hon. senator who sponsored this measure moved third reading of the bill. The whole performance takes less than half a column of Senate Hansard.
1 feel that the members of this chamber must not make the mistake of passing any measure of this sort without some of the government members standing up and offering one good reason as to why in their opinion the members of this house should support it. In my view it is quite significant that the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond and the hon. member for Hastings South felt the proposition was such that they could not go back to face their electors without having made some effort to modify this measure. I must confess that the members of our group could not go along with the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond. We could not see that his proposal would in any way improve the measure before us. But the fact that these two hon. members-and they were supported by some other members on the government side-did feel that in the committee they should register their protest, makes it apparent that we should have a good look at it.

I admit that the splitting of these shares in itself will not necessarily result in these prices going up, but with an estimated $10 million net clear this year for distribution, coupled with the fact that if this share split goes through we are going to have an increase in the selling price of these shares, it all indicates we should look at the measure carefully. There will be some people who will take their losses. Again, there is no law in Canada that says it is illegal for citizens to play the stock market. But I submit that it certainly is not in the public interest for the parliament of Canada to give its approval to a proposal of this sort without realizing the full implication, that this is a clear invitation to the people of Canada to try to get something for nothing; to get in on what is a very profitable venture before this company is declared a public carrier.
This company are able to take advantage of the fact that there is a crisis in Suez. They are able to use this as an excuse to come to parliament and ask that their shares be split five to one.
May I call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

Mr. Chairman, when the bill was before the house for second reading I did not take part in the debate because hon. members of this group who were on the committee which examined the bill were more
Private Bill
familiar with its provisions than I was; but I think there is one thing which is now evident, and it is that the object of the bill as it is explained in the explanatory note is certainly not the object in reality. Considering today's debate on this matter I believe the sponsor of the bill would be well advised to withdraw this legislation and wait until such time as the real intentions of this company are made known.
So far the discussion has proved beyond any doubt that the only possible effect the passage of this bill could have would be to promote inflation or, as far as this house is concerned, to condone gambling. There seems to be no other explanation for it. I think it strikes at a rather basic principle so far as we are concerned, because any legislation that comes before this house, particularly if it deals with private concerns as this does, must be judged first and foremost by the criterion of public interest.
As members of this house and as representatives of the people we cannot be concerned with the financial welfare of any particular firm. We must be concerned with the public interest first of all; and since there is nothing in this bill that commends itself in respect to the public interest then there is in effect no reason at all why this bill should be before the house, and it should therefore be withdrawn.
Certain of the information that has come out in our discussion has changed the minds of at least some hon. members of this house. I recall that not so long ago-as a matter of fact on February 26 of this year-when the hon. member for Bow River spoke on the second reading of this bill he took a very different attitude toward it from that revealed in his speech today. In fact he made certain statements at that time which one could only take as meaning that he was in support of the bill; but having been on the committee and having received certain information which in his own opinion would have been desirable to be made known to all members of this house, he has now entirely changed his view and has attacked the bill in terms which he himself deplored as recently as February 26. I am not saying this to be at all critical of the hon. member, because I think he is to be commended for his change of attitude.
On February 26, when referring to some of the speeches made by my colleagues, the hon. member for Bow River used the following words as reported at page 1679 of Hansard:
There have been a lot of things said in the debate on the bill, particularly since the moving of the amendment, which I personally cannot take to be true.

Today, however, the hon. member confirmed every one of those statements. He followed up the comment I just read by saying:
I am convinced that some of the statements that have been made have been grossly exaggerated.
Yet today he not only confirmed the statements that had been made at that time by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, who has taken an active part in this debate and by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. As a matter of fact he added some of his own comments in condemnation of this bill in much stronger terms than those used on that occasion.
This is a strong indication to me, Mr. Chairman, that those hon. members who had grave doubts about the wisdom of passing this bill have had their views fully confirmed, and those who were not quite sure where they stood with regard to the bill-as far as this side of the house is concerned at least-have now come down on the side opposing the bill. Considering the fact that since this debate commenced today not one member on the government side of the house and not even the sponsor of the bill has seen fit to take the floor to say anything in its favour, it appears to be a clear indication that they have not found very much to say in its favour, and certainly they have not made any attempt whatever to relate this bill to the public interest.
Considering that important fact, and considering that the members of the government themselves have not taken any part-as a matter of fact they appeared quite embarrassed by the whole thing-I think it would be the better part of wisdom for the sponsor to withdraw this bill and serve notice on the company unless they have reasons which can more readily commend themselves to the intelligence of hon. members of the house than the reason they have offered, then they should not be asking this house to condone their speculative manipulations.
I hope the sponsor of the bill or some other member on that side of the house who is anxious to get this bill through will tell us what is the reason that members on the Liberal side are so anxious to see this bill passed.
They have not yet given us any reason other than what is contained in the explanatory note as to why this legislation should be passed by this house. One cannot help but wonder what is the cause of the great anxiety. If there is anything hidden which they have not revealed, this would be the time to reveal it. I think it is due this committee that we should know why the Liberal members have taken it upon themselves and
[Mr. Zaplitny.l
feel it is their responsibility as public representatives to pilot through this house for a private company a bill which can only have the effect of putting that company in a better position to manipulate its stock on the market and make a profit. As a matter of fact, this seems to be a sort of pipe-line year. First the government get tangled up to their ears in a pipe line, and they have scarcely emerged from that when some of the members on the Liberal side have become tied up with a private bill for another pipe line. That is a very interesting angle which enters into the whole price arrangements of this company. So far not one word has been said on this point by the sponsor of this bill or by any of the hon. gentlemen across the way who seem to be most intimate with this company.
Then we come to the explanation given by the company, and that in itself constitutes

a very suspicious situation. They come to this parliament and say the reason they want this bill passed to permit them to split their shares five to one is, to use their own words, so they can effect a wider distribution of their shares. The evidence in the committee, so far as I have been able to find out, was to the effect that they have no intention whatever of placing more of their stock on the market. The two things simply do not go together. If the company was anxious to effect a wider distribution of their stockholdings in the hands of the public they have in their treasury 3,500,000 shares which could be placed on the market today without any legislation whatsoever. That is provided for in their charter. Why are they not doing that? Because, to use their own evidence, they do not require any extra capital. In their own opinion their capital is quite sufficient for their purposes. Certainly the return on that capital in the last couple of years has been very good, and they have no desire to change that situation.
What would be the purpose of splitting the shares other than to inflate the value of the shares to the extent of being able to make a capital gain? I am very doubtful, even if this company were to place extra shares on the market, that that would be such a good thing, because the time might come when the government would want to take over this particular pipe line as a public utility. I realize that is not the present intention, but the time may come.
We have had experience in the past of what can happen when a private company or group of companies operating a public utility reach the stage when they want that utility taken over as a public undertaking. In the meantime they have inflated or watered their stock to such an extent that the stockholdings do not represent the real value. We had that situation develop in this country in connection with our railroads. The Canadian National Railways was a sort of amalgamation or basket deal made up of a number of so-called bankrupt private companies which were taken over by the government after their stock had been inflated to a fantastic degree. As a matter of fact one of the great disabilities of the Canadian National Railways is the enormous amount of interest, amounting to around $20 million, which must be paid by the people of Canada every year on that inflated, valueless, watered stock which was taken over in the formation of the Canadian National Railways.
The same trend is developing with other public utilities, and the time may come when it will be desirable to take this company over as a public utility, and we may then find that 82715-132

There remains only one reason, the reason stated by members of the Social Credit group and by my colleagues. That is that this move is an attempt to put the company into a position where it will be able to make a capital gain at the expense of the consumers of its products or of the public generally who see fit to participate in the stockholdings.
Since that seems to be firmly established, since the sponsor of this bill and those hon. members who are supporting it have not come up with another explanation and certainly have not disproved the one which has been placed before the committee, I cannot imagine that the members of the Liberal party will sit back and use their steamroller majority as an argument - that is all they have used so far; they have not presented any other argument whatever during this debate-or sit back and act as a number of rubber stamps in order to do something to the advantage of a private company, which is not in the public interest. In the meantime I feel it is the duty of our colleagues and of all members on the opposition side-I invite my good friends to the right to participate- to oppose this bill until we get a satisfactory explanation.

Mr. Chairman and gentlemen, it is my pleasure to present to you this amending bill respecting Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company. The purpose of the bill is to change the stock structure.
[Mr. Gauthier (Portneuf) .1
When the company was organized in 1951 it was authorized to issue five million shares without nominal or par value. Because of the success of the company the officers felt it necessary and wise to change that structure. They are seeking authority to change it to this effect: that instead of issuing five million shares without nominal or par value they should be allowed to subdivide the shares so that there will be 25 millions without nominal or par value. The purpose is to make the shares more readily available to the investing public. It is felt that because the price of the shares on the market has risen so greatly, the small investor would be more inclined to purchase shares if they were reduced in price.
That was, in essence, the argument presented when this bill came before that committee. A great deal has been said about that reason, or the absurdity of that reason; yet no one on the government side of the house has yet made any effort whatsoever to explain or defend in any way a statement such as the one I have just placed on the record.
Now, it seems rather strange that this company should be showing so much concern about the small investor when the same company, as a matter of deliberate policy, sought to exclude the general public from ownership and control of the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company. We know from page 91 of the committee report of March 19, 1951, when Mr. R. L. Bridges, a director of the Bechtel Corporation of the United States outlined to the committee the proposed capital structure of the new company, what the situation was. It is important to bear these facts in mind when we hear these rather naive statements that the company's main concern is to provide for greater public participation in its financing.
At that time, in 1951, Mr. Bridges pointed out that the total cost of the line was set at approximately $86,700,000 and the distribution of this amount among common shares, bonds, and debentures was in the following order: $30 million of first mortgage bonds to be sold to institutional investors in Canada; some $36 million, in United States dollars, first mortgage bonds to be sold to institutional investors in the United States; and approximately $14 million worth of debentures and $7 million worth of common stock.
So here is a company which arranges its financing, when it builds a pipe line with borrowed money, so that the general public will not have any opportunity whatsoever of playing a real part in this venture because, of course, by this arrangement they exclude those who are putting up the money from having any share in the control or management of the company. And here is a company which deliberately sets out to exclude the general public, and to confine equity

capital to some 8 per cent, the balance being money borrowed. In this situation, Mr. Chairman, it seems rather strange that now we should be told that this company is so much concerned about permitting people generally to participate in its affairs. We know more than that-

That is a matter of the over-all financing of the company.
A question then asked was:
I think that is one of the main issues at stake?
The answer was:
I don't think it has anything to do with the actual splitting of the stock. It is the opinion of our financial advisers that if they were at about one-fifth of their value they would have a wider distribution.
Mr. McQuarrie quoted a story that his secretary would love to buy some of the stock in Trans Mountain, but that at $100 a share she could not do so. If the price were to be cut, though, people would be willing to buy 20 shares at $10, or $15, or $20.
If the company were really so solicitous about the welfare of this secretary they could have arranged to provide her and other members of the general public with shares at the time the company's shares were first on 82715-132i

the market; but, as I suggested earlier, as a matter of deliberate policy they prevented members of the general public from participating in the affairs of the company.
The continued line of questioning will indicate some of the factors which were brought out before the committee, and these are matters which I think every member of this house should seriously consider before passing judgment on this legislation.
Q. If you obtain permission to divide these shares, that would mean that the three million-odd shares held by the company would be multiplied by five?
Now those are held solely by the company and when those are put on the market the value will increase to some extent. What position does that leave the company in financially?
A. We do not know if they will ever be put on the market.
Q. If you are going to have 15 million held by the company surely you would put some of those on the market?
A. Not necessarily.
Just reflect for a moment. Here is a company which professes to be concerned about the right of the general public to buy shares in the company; yet its officers say that after the stock split the shares now held by the company are not necessarily going to be put on the market. Then what is the objective behind this legislation? It certainly cannot involve any benefit to the general public.
The evidence I have placed on the record indicates one of the reasons why members of the house are not prepared to pass judgment on the legislation until such time as they have been able to examine that evidence very carefully. We have heard repeated statements that this is a very simple bill, that the only reason the company is coming before parliament and asking for this amendment is that it wants to split its shares to enable the general public to reap some benefit. But there has never been any evidence given in the house or any evidence given in the committee to indicate that there is any validity in the argument put forward by the company or the sponsors of the bill.
These rather bland assurances are not borne out by the facts. I do not think anyone is going to be so naive as to think this company or any other company is going to allow its over-all policies to be guided by the desire to do something in the general good. Private companies are in business to make money. The directors of those companies are there to produce the maximum by way of return to the shareholders, and they will tell you that if they do not do the job they are not going to remain as directors. But to ex-' pect us to believe thht the only reason this company is coming before parliament is its desire to help the general public is a lot of nonsense.

Private Bill
It is quite obvious that the motive behind the stock split is to enable the company to realize additional capital gains. They know, and I think it is generally accepted, that when shares go beyond $100 they do not trade as freely on the market. There is less buying and selling and, of course, when you reduce the amount of buying and selling you reduce the opportunities for making capital gains. The company realizes that through a stock split and through a greater movement of company shares those who hold shares are going to be in a better position to gain financially.
We know that if in a year or so from now the company under its present capital structure is making, shall we say, $5 on an original $10 share, naturally it will look like a very substantial profit; but if they can split the shares into five and make it appear as though they are only making $1 a share, then the general public will be free to believe that the company is not making as much money as it actually is. It is simply a question of trying to hoodwink the public, to create the illusion that the company is not making as much money out of the general public as the facts show.
It is quite obvious that any company which undertakes to split its stock on this basis is doing so because it feels it to be in the interests of the financial position of the company, and that is the only reason. Therefore when we have a company like Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company coming before parliament and asking that parliament amend its original charter, I think we have to ask ourselves whether parliament exists in order to provide opportunities for private companies to make money at the expense of the general public.
When the company came before parliament to get its original charter its officers made certain commitments. I understand that the hon. member for Bumaby-Richmond made some reference to a speech he made when the legislation first came before the house. I am sure that he and other members from British Columbia were under the impression that the company was going to do a great service to the people of the lower mainland. It was going to build a pipe line and provide increased employment in that part of Canada, and it was going to result in a tremendous enlargement of refining capacity. Of course it is the old, old story. While there has perhaps been an increase in the refining capacity, that may not be due to the pipe line itself.
In my own province we have enjoyed a great increase in refining capacity, more than double, in the years since 1951, because of the increased consumption of gasoline and other

oil products, but we have to be very careful in considering this bill dealing with a pipe line because we have had our fingers burned too often. We have accepted assurances from these people. They have come before parliament and have appeared before the committee. They have made certain commitments and promises, yet their promises are seldom if ever fulfilled. Surely we ought to profit from our experience with Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, a company which also came to parliament with all sorts of commitments and raring to go. They could get all kinds of capital. All they wanted was a charter and the O.K, of the board of transport commissioners, and they were all set to build a pipe line. We know the sordid story there. It well behooves members of the house to look very carefully at pipeline legislation brought before the house.
I ask all members before passing judgment on the legislation to ask themselves whether the objective behind the bill is a worthy and sound one, whether it is a question of satisfying the interests of the Canadian people as a whole or whether it is simply a question of facilitating the ability of a particular company to split its stock with the hope of making more money in the years that lie ahead. We know this company has certainly made a considerable amount of money since it was formed. I think it was admitted by the officers of the company in the committee that their profits for the last year were just under $7 million, and it is likely that their profits will be much higher in the next year when the figures are announced.
It is a very lucrative company, and it is quite evident under the circumstances that a stock split is going to redound to the advantage of the shareholders and directors of the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company. Is it not rather significant that the time the company declares its first dividend of $1 a share is precisely the time it decides it wants to split its stock? The officers of the company know that with the split in the stock and with increased dividends, the price of the stock is going to go up. Therefore it is to the advantage of those who now hold stock in the company to push for this split in the stock, because they tend to gain a great deal in the form of capital gains. I think it is pure, simple economics and you have to consider the situation from that standpoint.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
It would appear to me that you might, in the foreseeable future, be able to pay a profit of probably $10 per share if you continued to improve your position in the next few years as much as you have done in the past few years. But even on the basis of the figures you have given, a net profit of $10 million on $1,500,000 would appear to be an embarrassing dividend to be reporting to the public. I think this matter of public relations will be involved in the fact that for every $10 share which the shareholder takes in 1959 there is to be a dividend of $10 per year, so it would appear to me.
And so the evidence comes out, Mr. Chairman, that the company itself cannot refute the argument that the possibility of their making tremendous profits is a real one. The purpose of this bill is to hand over to the company an opportunity to amass capital gains, the ultimate end of which will be that people are going to get something for nothing; and since this is of course impossible the public will have to pay. As long as capitalism is allowed to go on with this kind of thing the public is going to pay through the nose until some day the situation, with all its inflation, will bring its reward to the Canadian people. If this continues, then ultimately it will break. What we have been saying here today will come true, and the wrongs that have been perpetrated in this house will reap their reward.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since I began following this discussion this afternoon, a very interesting document has come into my hands, as I believe it has come into the hands of other hon. members of the house. I refer to the annual report of the governor of the Bank of Canada to the Minister of Finance for the year 1956. Some of the statements in this report seem to me quite relevant to the situation we now have under discussion.

As hon. members will recall, this afternoon I had some remarks to make on what relation this proposal before us has to the present inflationary pressures within our economy, and as hon. members who have looked at this report at all will realize, considerable reference is made to that subject by the governor of the Bank of Canada. I think this report is of some interest because, among other things, it sets forth on one of its pages the preamble to the Bank of Canada Act, and if we were to judge the views that are held by hon. members opposite, in spite of their silence as far as formal speeches are concerned, by a number of the interjections which have been made, one could conceive that this bill had as its purpose something that I will attempt to set forth by a rather free quotation from this preamble to the Bank of Canada Act.
I think if we were to take the bill we have before us and relate it to that preamble it might go something like this, according to views of Liberal members opposite who seem prepared to support the bill:
Whereas it is desirable ... to regulate credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of the nation, to control and protect the external value of the national monetary unit, and to mitigate by its influence fluctuations in the general level of production, trade, prices and employment . . . and generally promote the economic and financial welfare of the dominion: Therefore-
And I move to the bill:
Therefore Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada enacts as follows:
Each of the five million shares without nominal or par value constituting the capital stock of Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company, whether such share is issued or unissued, is hereby subdivided into five shares . . .
And so on. As far as I have been able to deduce the attitude of hon. members who are prepared to support this bill, that appears to be the appreciation they have of the purposes of the sort of proposal we have before us. If any of those hon. members feel that this is not a fair summary of their views on the value of this sort of bill, I hope they will get up and correct me; because the question of whether or not this bill is in the general interests of the people of Canada is, as some of my colleagues have suggested, the question that should be paramount in our minds when we come to consider approving or disapproving it.
As far as I am concerned I think one or two of the statements in the report by the governor of the Bank of Canada have a direct bearing on the situation as I understand it and as I attempted to outline it earlier this afternoon. On page 22 of the report, for example, I find this:
82715-133J
Private Bill
Money and credit not based on real savings have no real value for the community as a whole, and since one unit of money in one man's hands or bank account is indistinguishable from another unit of money in another man's hands or bank account, the worthless element in an excessive supply of money or credit dilutes the real value of money in everyone's hands and bank accounts, and of all money payments to be received in the future.
I submit Mr. Chairman, that the opinion expressed by the governor of the Bank of Canada certainly bears out the argument I was attempting to advance this afternoon, when I was pointing out that the tremendously inflated value of the stock of this company over its real value has created what to my mind is worthless purchasing power. In other words it does not represent any real increase in the wealth of this country; and for that reason, as is suggested in this report, it does dilute the money of all the rest of us, and it puts those of us who have to depend on money we earn to buy the things we need in the position of competing with those who have these worthless dollars; worthless, at least, in the real sense of the word but which have, as the governor points out, just as much purchasing power as the dollars a man gets in his pay cheque at the end of the week after working in a mine in the constituency of the hon. member for Kootenay East.

I did not follow that. I am
sorry.

speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member will take the trouble to read my speech at his leisure later.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: If it is not any clearer than what you are saying it will not be worth while.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: It is just for intelligent people. You could not follow it.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
If these excess dollars have been created by the inflationary process and the rise in the price of this stock, and we are then asked to accede to a further step which will increase that inflationary process, we will be aiding and abetting the very problem that is outlined by the governor of the Bank of Canada in his annual report this year. He says, as found at page 13 of the report:
During 1956 the Canadian economy was subject to serious inflationary pressures. While physical output expanded by the unusually large increment of 7 per cent over 1955, the money value of expenditures on goods and services grew even more rapidly.
I submit that one of the reasons the money value of goods and services grew more rapidly than the physical output is that the people who own these pipe-line companies, among a great many others, are allowed to go on with this process of filching unearned dollars from

Private Bill
the Canadian economy. I submit that when the governor of the Bank of Canada draws to our attention, as he does in this report, the problem which has been created by the rapid expansion in consumer credit through the finance companies he is confirming what I attempted to suggest briefly this afternoon. He is confirming that because the working people generally in this country are not receiving in real value a return for their work, and are forced to go in increasing measure to the finance companies to purchase the goods they consider they need, we are now faced with the problem outlined by the governor of the Bank of Canada, and everything I attempted to argue earlier to the effect that the kind of action contemplated by this company is adding to this problem is borne out in the report which we received this afternoon.
As I said earlier, there is no guarantee that after this stock split is approved, if the house persists in approving it, the split shares will continue to rise in the stock market. However, in view of the evidence presented to us earlier by the hon. member for Vancouver East as to what happened in the past and what had been discovered on the basis of a very serious and detailed investigation of the situation, in my opinion those of us who suggest that the past history of oil companies will likely be repeated in the case of this oil company are not very far from the mark.
Granted that the present physical expansion of industrial capacity continues at the rate suggested by the governor of the Bank of Canada, we can reasonably expect that the predictions made in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines by the officers of the company as to the anticipated output of the pipe line, or perhaps I should say throughput, will come true and that the growing profit position which they suggested they expect will in fact come about. That being the case, the trading that will go on after these shares are split will result in a continued rise in their value on the stock market.
I am not sure that the figures with respect to the increase in the number of barrels of oil carried by the line have been set forth yet, and I think they might be of interest to members of the house generally who were not on the committee in order that they may have some idea of just what is happening. We had outlined to us the number of barrels put through the line destined for Canadian refineries on the coast of British Columbia, the number of barrels going to United States refineries through the so-called spur line, and some figures as to the oil loaded on tankers for shipment overseas or down the California coast.

In 1953 the company put through the line 16,739 barrels per day, all to Canadian refineries. That was for only part of the year. In 1954 the figure rose to 37,296 barrels per day, all to British Columbia refineries. In 1955 they put through 52,902 barrels per day to Canadian refineries and 31,080 barrels per day to the United States. In 1956 they put through 59,590 barrels per day to Canadian refineries, 52,490 barrels per day to the United States and 17,023 barrels were loaded on tankers for shipment offshore. We were informed that most of the last amount went to California.
In the year 1956 we find that 46.1 per cent of the oil going through the line went to refineries in British Columbia, 40.7 per cent to refineries in the United States just over the Canadian border, and 13.2 per cent of the oil was shipped by tanker, most of it to California.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: So we made most of our money from the Americans.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Some tankers went to Japan and one to France, I believe. Then we come to the oil movement during 1957. In January of this year the figure was 71,150 barrels per day to Canadian refineries, 84,859 barrels per day to United States refineries, and 33,368 barrels loaded in tankers. So we can see that the plan they have, on the basis of orders for the transportation of oil from the oil companies, indicates that the capacity is growing and also that the percentage of oil that is being shipped across the line to the United States in raw form is also increasing so that it becomes well over 50 per cent of the total in the current year.
One reason I have set forth these figures, Mr. Chairman, is that they bear out what some of us, before we went into the committee, had heard was likely to take place, namely that some expansion and doubling of the capacity of this line was contemplated by the company. That fact was borne out in the evidence given to us in the committee by the officers of the company. They pointed out that their plans called for a process of what they call looping-I believe that is the term- so that for certain sections between certain pumping stations they will have actually two lines, and with increased pumping capacity in the pumping stations they will be able to increase the amount of oil flowing through the line.
That being the case, Mr. Chairman, I must say that when we got into the standing committee on this bill and had an opportunity of discussing this question in detail with the officers of the company, I fully and honestly expected they would tell the committee that the real reason behind their request for this

splitting of shares and their claim that they wanted to distribute the stock more widely was that they expected to have large capital expenditures in the expansion of the line, and that therefore they wanted to be in a position to put more of their stock from the treasury of the company before the public.
If that had been the case, then I would say the argument that the present market price of the shares of $117 is a little high for them to be easily traded on the market might have had some real validity. As I say, Mr. Chairman, I was really shocked when we got into the committee to discover that the officers of the company categorically denied that they had any intention, as far as they knew at the present time or as far as any plans they had at the present time were concerned, of putting any of the shares from the treasury on the market. They informed us that all their current financing program for capital expansion had been raised very nicely, thank you, through the sale of fixed-interest securities; that they had no desire to offer or any intention of offering any shares from the treasury to the public; that as far as they could see they were not going to need to offer the shares to the public; and that as long as their present successful operation continued they expected to be able to do any financing they might require by the sale of debenture securities.
I must say, Mr. Chairman, that if before we got into the committee I had-as I did have-grave doubts about the wisdom of this measure being brought before parliament, those doubts were certainly multiplied a hundredfold when we were confronted with that bald admission from the officers of the company that as far as the company itself was concerned they had no requirement whatever for this stock-splitting move. As was suggested in some of the evidence that was placed in detail before the committee by the hon. member for Yorkton, it reached the point where the officers of the company in effect were telling the committee that they "didn't know nuttin' from nuttin' ". They refused categorically to agree that any of the possible explanations that members of the committee offered for their actions were correct; but on the other hand they were extremely careful not to deny that some of our deductions were correct.
In the end we were left with the rather surprising announcement that was made to us early in the proceedings, namely that the real purpose of this was simply a matter of their public relations. Yet they would not even admit for whom those public relations were designed. I think any member who, when he has the opportunity, will carefully read through the minutes of proceedings and
Private Bill
evidence of those two sittings of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines-

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Ten minutes to go.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
-if he will approach the matter with an open mind, as I am sure the hon. member for York-Scarborough will, will be driven to the conclusion that what companies like the Trans Mountain Oil PipeLine Company call public relations is simply a successful camouflaging from the general public of the profits they are making, and a successful attempt to create in the minds-of the public of Canada the idea that somehow or other they are shareholders and participators in what they call this great free enterprise system.
This company has also followed a dodge that a number of corporations follow today, namely making it possible for a few of their employees to have a certain nominal interest in the shares of the company. This is a part of public relations. As a matter of fact, if the hon. member for York-Scarborough would really like to learn something about public relations, particularly in the political field, in view of what may take place before too long, I would suggest that he read a book called "The Golden Kazoo" which gives quite a little sermon on the matter of public relations, particularly in the political field in which, of course, he has some small interest.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Why not quote "Salvation Island"?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
It sets forth rather neatly the modem technique of so-called public relations which has been employed with some considerable degree of success by companies like Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company and which apparently is going to be developed and expanded for the benefit of some of the entrenched political pipe-line companies that we have in the country.
So, as I say, I hope hon. members will read the minutes of the committee. Some of us have attempted, as far as we have been able to do so, to bring to light what took place there; to bring to light the fact that the proceedings of that committee verified and jusified the opposition that we in this group had to this bill at second reading; justified our suggestion that the subject matter of this bill should have been referred to the committee for study before it was approved in principle; and justified our suggestion now that this bill should never get beyond this committee of the whole to the house with the Speaker in the chair.
I hope something may come out of this debate, even though it may appear to have

been a little one-sided. It is rather difficult, you know, to get into full swing of debate when the only * thing one has to debate is the odd interjection by a member like the hon. member for Kootenay East, who simply says he cannot follow one's argument but makes no attempt to get up and put forward an argument of his own.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: As my colleague the hon. member for Comox-Alberni pointed out just now, since this debate started this afternoon every member of the house has received a very important document. I am not very optimistic that this document or the message it brings to Canadian parliamentarians will have any great effect on the government benches. I may say I am completely without any optimism that it will have any effect on those in this house who support the government.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: To what one are you referring, "Salvation Island"?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
No, I am not
referring to "Salvation Island", but perhaps that is the literary level of the hon. member for Kootenay East. I can quite understand that an erudite document prepared by an extremely able public servant would be beyond his powers of comprehension, but there are members in this house who, I think, could learn from this statement of Mr. J. E. Coyne which has been presented to us today. If they are not able to digest it in the form in which it has been presented to

parliament, perhaps they could take some advantage of a few items from the report that appeared in tonight's Ottawa Journal.
This brings before us, in connection with this bill, a condition that is possibly as grave as has been faced in the Canadian economy in the last 20 years. It is not for nothing that a public servant of Mr. Coyne's calibre suggests nothing less than reorganization of the character of Canada's banking system in order to cope with the still unsolved problem of growing inflation in this country. Mr. Coyne has considered it necessary to warn us that we have not yet coped with the dangerous inflationary situation which existed during 1956.
In that connection, sir, I consider that this bill should receive very serious and grave consideration by the members of this house, not the rather light-hearted and flippant attitude we have been observing the last few hours. There can be no doubt about it; if this company and similar companies in the country are permitted to carry out these stock market manoeuvres such as are envisaged in this bill, then they will contribute to the situation that is causing so much concern to Mr. Coyne and his economic experts. He mentions in this report on page 31 the very serious competition for money and resources that has been going on in Canada for the last two years. He says:
In any condition of an excess of physical demand over physical supply, some elements of demand must of necessity give way, lose out to others. Competition for money with higher interest rates produces fewer casualties and less social stress than unrestricted competition for goods with higher prices. Better a rise in the price of borrowed money (and so a stimulus to those who save) than a very great rise in the price of goods and housing, in the cost of schools and hospitals and public utilities, and in the cost of production of exporting and all other industries throughout the nation-
Now, if there is any measure that has come before us, Mr. Chairman, which is designed to raise the cost of goods, to raise the cost of production of all other industries, it is this measure that is before us today. We have heard from the officers of the company that the book value of the shares now outstanding is some $21 million; the present market value is in the neighbourhood of $175 million, rather in excess of $175 million. This inflation of values, sir, has been caused by the inordinate profit rate obtained by this company during the last two years and the expectation of still more inordinate profits in the future.
In order that these profits may escape unnoticed by the general public, and in particular by the growing number of Canadians

who depend on crude oil products for heating, cooking and other domestic activities, and the growing number of industries that are dependent upon oil products as a source of energy, the company is requesting this stock split. The whole effect of this bill will be to cause inflation of consumer costs and to contribute to the inflationary situation that now afflicts us.
I think we have to bear in mind that this is an inflated value, and it is caused entirely by the tremendous profit situation of this company and its expectation of even greater profits in the future. We must dismiss, Mr. Chairman, if we lay any claim whatever to intelligence, as sheer nonsense the proposals put forward by the officers of this company suggesting that they are concerned with public relations; that they are concerned to have a wide distribution of their stock. This is a piece of arrant nonsense which will not stand
Business of the House
investigation, because they give us no evidence whatever that the existing stock is going to go on the market.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

speechtext:
1.	Does the federal government co-operate with the city of Halifax or any other Nova Scotia municipality in slum clearance and in building units for cheap ($25 to $35) rental?
2.	If so, to what degree?
Answer by: Hon. Roberi H. Winters (Minister of Public Works):
The federal government in 1952 entered into an agreement with the province of Nova Scotia and the city of Halifax for the purpose of constructing 161 low rental housing units in Halifax under section 36 of the National Housing Act. Pursuant to this section the federal government assumed 75 per cent of the capital cost of the project and undertook to bear a like share of operating deficits. This project was completed and fully occupied by the end of 1953. The units are rented to
Questions
families having an annual income of not less than $1,500 and not more than $3,240. Rents are graded in accordance with the size and income of the tenant families and, on the average, families pay rents approximating 20 per cent of their income.
The federal government by agreement with the province of Nova Scotia and the Nova Scotia housing commission has provided financial assistance under section 36 of the act to co-operative organizations throughout the province for the construction of 240 units of home-ownership housing in the municipalities of Amherst, Antigonish, Halifax, North Sydney, Sydney, Trenton, Wolfville and Yarmouth.
On June 7, 1956, an order in council was passed authorizing Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to make a grant to the city of Halifax under section 33 of the National Housing Act, amounting to $12,000. This grant was intended to cover three-quarters of the cost of an urban renewal study to be carried out by the city.
